messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Parole Officer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

Vignette:
Kofi is a 34-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a parole officer in a mid-sized city in the Midwest. He came to the clinic quietly, arriving early and choosing a seat facing the door, and it was several minutes before he made sustained eye contact with the intake coordinator. He described himself, with some difficulty, as someone who had "been through something that men aren't supposed to talk about," and the shame embedded in that phrase seemed to organize much of what followed.

For approximately two years, Kofi was in a relationship with a woman he had met through mutual friends. The abuse began gradually — verbal at first, then physical — and escalated over the course of eighteen months into repeated incidents of serious violence. The episode that brought him to emergency care occurred when his partner struck him across the face with a ceramic object during an argument, fracturing his orbital bone and lacerating his cheek. He was taken by ambulance to the local hospital, where he spent several hours in the emergency department. He remembers lying on the gurney, the fluorescent lights above him, the sharp chemical smell of antiseptic filling his nostrils, and the taste of blood sitting heavy on the back of his tongue. He remembers the sound of his partner's voice still ringing in his ears — her words, her tone — even as nurses moved around him. He did not report the assault to police. He told the hospital staff he had fallen.

In the months that followed, Kofi ended the relationship but found that the event had not ended inside him. The smell of antiseptic — encountered now in the supply room at the correctional facility where he supervises parolees, where cleaning products line the shelves — can stop him mid-step, his body flooding with a sensation he describes as the memory arriving whole, not as a recollection but as a recurrence. He hears her voice in those moments. He can taste blood. What frightens him most is that it does not feel like the past; it feels like something still happening, something he has not yet survived.

His work requires him to meet with parolees one-on-one, many of whom are men, and Kofi had come to believe that being alone with any man constituted a situation he could not safely navigate. He began scheduling his individual sessions with male clients during open office hours, ensuring colleagues were always nearby, and he restructured his caseload without formally explaining why. He carries himself through the workday with a vigilance that exhausts him — watching faces for microshifts in expression, reading body language for what he is certain are early signals of danger. When a male client looks at him in a way he perceives as appraising or objectifying, something tightens in his chest that he cannot easily name or dismiss.

Outside of work, Kofi has pulled away from his partner of eighteen months, a woman he describes as patient and loving. He had come to push warmth away when he felt it — not because he distrusted her specifically, but because positive feeling had come to seem like exposure, like a lowering of a guard he was not sure he could afford to lower. He avoids disagreements with her entirely, conceding in conversations where he once would have engaged, because any hint of escalating tension now feels to him like the edge of something catastrophic. She has noticed. She has asked. He has not been able to explain.

Kofi has told almost no one what his former partner did to him. He is certain that what happened was profoundly unjust and equally certain that nothing will ever be done about it — that the system he works within daily would not have taken him seriously, that people would have questioned the story. He does not say his life has been destroyed lightly; he says it with the flat affect of someone reporting a fact. He is not sure, on some days, that he wants to continue. It was this last recognition — arriving with increasing frequency — that finally brought him to seek help. What he hopes for, expressed haltingly at the end of the intake session, is to feel like himself again. What he fears is that the person he was before no longer exists to return to.
